Shobach
shō´băk
n. (captain of the host of Hadarezer, slain by David)
Hebrew Shobak, of uncertain meaning; the Chronicler spells it Shophach. He commanded the Syrian army brought from beyond the river to fight Israel, and he died in the battle.

Biblical Definition

Beaten once, the Syrians escalated: “And Hadarezer sent, and brought out the Syrians that were beyond the river: and they came to Helam; and Shobach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them” (2 Samuel 10:16). The result is recorded without suspense: “And the Syrians fled before Israel; and David slew the men of seven hundred chariots of the Syrians, and forty thousand horsemen, and smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there” (2 Samuel 10:18). The consequence was political: “And when all the kings that were servants to Hadarezer saw that they were smitten before Israel, they made peace with Israel, and served them. So the Syrians feared to help the children of Ammon any more” (2 Samuel 10:19). The war had begun over an insult — Hanun had shaved David's ambassadors and cut off their garments — and it ended with the Syrian confederacy dismantled. The next verse of the narrative is the one that matters most, because it opens the chapter of David's great fall: “And it came to pass, after the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, that David sent Joab, and his servants with him, and all Israel; and they destroyed the children of Ammon, and besieged Rabbah. But David tarried still at Jerusalem” (2 Samuel 11:1).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Shobach; the name belongs to the captain of the Syrian host under Hadarezer, slain in battle with David.

expand to see more

SHOBACH, n. The captain of the host of Hadarezer, king of Zobah, slain in battle by David's army.

HOST, n. An army; a number of men embodied for war; a great multitude.

SYRIA, n. A country of Asia, north of Palestine, whose kings were frequently at war with Israel.

AMBASSADOR, n. A minister of the highest rank, employed by one prince or state at the court of another.

CONFEDERACY, n. A league or covenant between persons or states for mutual support.

Modern Corruption

Military success is read as the measure of a king's standing with God, when the narrative sets David's greatest victory immediately before his greatest sin.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the arrangement of the narrative. Chapter 10 ends with the Syrian confederacy broken, Shobach dead, and every vassal king suing for peace — the high-water mark of David's reign. Chapter 11 begins with the words at the time when kings go forth to battle, and records that David sent Joab and tarried still at Jerusalem. The historian does not comment. He simply puts the two paragraphs side by side, and the reader who has followed the victory feels the sentence land.

The lesson is one Scripture teaches repeatedly and the church forgets as often: danger follows success more reliably than it follows failure. Hezekiah's pride came after the Assyrian was turned back; Uzziah was marvellously helped till he was strong, and when he was strong his heart was lifted up to his destruction. Paul's warning is the plainest form of it — let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. Shobach fell at Helam and David fell in Jerusalem, and the second fall did more damage to Israel than the first army ever could.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Shobak (H7731), Shobach; Hadarezer (H1928), Hadarezer; sar tsaba (H8269, H6635), captain of the host; Aram (H758), Syria.

expand to see more

Hebrew Shobak (H7731) — Shobach, spelled Shophach in 1 Chronicles 19:16.

Hebrew Hadarezer (H1928) — Hadarezer, king of Zobah; also spelled Hadadezer.

Hebrew sar tsaba (H8269, H6635) — captain of the host, commander of the army.

Hebrew Aram (H758) — Syria, the Aramean confederacy beyond the river.

Hebrew nagaph (H5062) — to smite, strike down; the fate of the Syrian captain.

Usage

"“Shobach the captain of the host of Hadarezer went before them” — the Syrian commander."

"“Smote Shobach the captain of their host, who died there” — the battle at Helam."

"“But David tarried still at Jerusalem” — the sentence that follows the victory."
